entries.830f82d14431b8acb8c2df7852fe830ef82e3d31: <div sID="gen33566" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="2Pet.2" sID="2Pet.2"/> <div eID="gen33566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33567" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33568" type="x-p"/> The apostle, having in the foregoing chapter exhorted them to proceed and advance in the Christian race, now comes to remove, as much as in him lay, what he could not but apprehend would hinder their complying with his exhortation. He therefore gives them fair warning of false teachers, by whom they might be in danger of being seduced. To prevent this, I. He describes these seducers as impious in themselves, and very pernicious to others, <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.1-2Pet.2.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. He assures them of the punishment that shall be inflicted on them, <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.3-2Pet.2.6">ver. 3-6</reference>. III. He tells us how contrary the method is which God takes with those who fear him, <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.7-2Pet.2.9">ver. 7-9</reference>. IV. He fills up the rest of the chapter with a further description of those seducers of whom he would have them beware.
entries.5c12a89b1f843c3e7a53d7298a89c2a091c347e5: <div eID="gen33568" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33567" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">False Prophets and Corrupt Leaders. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 67.)</title> <div sID="gen33569" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> But there were false prophets also among the people, even as there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them, and bring upon themselves swift destruction. 2 And many shall follow their pernicious ways; by reason of whom the way of truth shall be evil spoken of. <hi type="super">3</hi> And through covetousness shall they with feigned words make merchandise of you— <div eID="gen33569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33570" type="x-p"/> I. In the end of the former chapter there is mention made of holy men of God, who lived in the times of the Old Testament, and were used as the amanuenses of the Holy Ghost, in writing the sacred oracles; but in the beginning of this he tells us they had, even at that time, false prophets in the church as well as true. In all ages of the church, and under all dispensations, when God sends true prophets, the devil sends some to seduce and deceive, false prophets in the Old Testament, and false Christs, false apostles, and seducing teachers, in the New. Concerning these observe, 1. Their business is to bring in destructive errors, <hi type="italic">even damnable heresies,</hi> as the business of teachers sent of God is to show the way of truth, even the true way to everlasting life. There are damnable heresies as well as damnable practices; and false teachers are industrious to spread pernicious errors. 2. Damnable heresies are commonly brought in privily, under the cloak and colour of truth. Those who introduce destructive heresies <hi type="italic">deny the Lord that bought them.</hi> They reject and refuse to hear and learn of the great teacher sent from God, though he is the only Saviour and Redeemer of men, who paid a price sufficient to redeem as many worlds of sinners as there are sinners in the world. 4. Those who bring in errors destructive to others bring swift (and therefore sure) <hi type="italic">destruction upon themselves.</hi> Self-destroyers are soon destroyed; and those who are so hardened as to propagate errors destructive to others shall surely and suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy. <div eID="gen33570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33571" type="x-p"/> II. He proceeds, in the <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.2">second verse</reference>, to tell us the consequence with respect to others; and here we may learn, 1. Corrupt leaders seldom fail of many to follow them; though the way of error is a pernicious way, yet many are ready to walk therein. Men drink in iniquity like water, and are pleased to live in error. <hi type="italic">The prophets prophesy falsely, and the people love to have it so.</hi> 2. The spreading of error will bring up an evil report on the way of truth; that is, the way of salvation by Jesus Christ, who is <hi type="italic">the way, the truth, and the life.</hi> The Christian religion is from the God of truth as the author, leads to true happiness in the enjoyment of the true God as the end, and works truth in the inward part as the means of acceptably serving God. And yet this way of truth is traduced and blasphemed by those who embrace and advance destructive errors. This the apostle has foretold as what should certainly come to pass. Let us not be offended at any thing of this in our day, but take care that we give no occasion to the enemy to blaspheme the holy name whereby we are called, or speak evil of that way whereby we hope to be saved. <div eID="gen33571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33572" type="x-p"/> III. Observe, in the next place, the method seducers take to draw disciples after them: they use <hi type="italic">feigned words;</hi> they flatter, and by good words and fair speeches deceive the hearts of the simple, inducing them to yield entirely to the opinions which these seducers endeavour to propagate, and sell and deliver themselves over to the instruction and government of these false teacher, who make a gain of those whom they make their proselytes, serving themselves and making some advantage of them; for all this is through covetousness, with a desire and design to get more wealth, or credit, or commendation, by increasing the number of their followers. The faithful ministers of Christ, who show men the way of truth, desire the profit and advantage of their followers, that they may be saved; but these seducing teachers desire and design only their own temporal advantage and worldly grandeur.
entries.72e5020bbe27e8b265d44036d2683b6986184aea: <div eID="gen33577" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Divine Judgments. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 67.)</title> <div sID="gen33578" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> And delivered just Lot, vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked: <hi type="super">8</hi> (For that righteous man dwelling among them, in seeing and hearing, vexed <hi type="italic">his</hi> righteous soul from day to day with <hi type="italic">their</hi> unlawful deeds;) 9 The Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly out of temptations, and to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished: <div eID="gen33578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33579" type="x-p"/> When God sends destruction on the ungodly, he commands deliverance for the righteous; and, if he rain fire and brimstone on the wicked, he will cover the head of the just, and they shall be hid in the day of his anger. This we have an instance of in his preserving Lot. Here observe, 1. The character given of Lot; he is called <hi type="italic">a just man;</hi> this he was as to the generally prevailing bent of his heart and through the main of his conversation. God does not account men just or unjust from one single act, but from their general course of life. And here is a just man in the midst of a most corrupt and profligate generation universally gone off from all good. He does not follow the multitude to do evil, but in a city of injustice he walks uprightly. 2. The impression the sins of others made upon this righteous man. Though the sinner takes pleasure in his wickedness, it is a grief and vexation to the soul of the righteous. In bad company we cannot escape either guilt or grief. Let the sins of others be a trouble to us, otherwise it will not be possible for us to keep ourselves pure. 3. Here is a particular mention of the duration and continuance of this good man's grief and vexation: it was <hi type="italic">from day to day.</hi> Being accustomed to hear and see their wickedness did not reconcile him to it, nor abate of the horror that was occasioned by it. This is the righteous man whom God preserved from the desolating judgment that destroyed all round about him. From this instance we are taught to argue that God knows how to deliver his people and punish his enemies. It is here presupposed that the righteous must have their temptations and trials. The devil and his instruments will thrust sore at them, that they may fall; and, if we will get to heaven, it must be through many tribulations. It is therefore our duty to reckon upon and prepare for them. Observe here, (1.) <hi type="italic">The Lord knows those that are his.</hi> He has set apart him who is godly for himself; and, if there is but one in five cities, he knows him; and where there is a greater number he cannot be ignorant of nor overlook any one of them. (2.) The wisdom of God is never at a loss about ways and means to deliver his people. They are often utterly at a loss, and can see no way; he can deliver a great many. (3.) The deliverance of the godly is the work of God, that which he concerns himself in, both his wisdom to contrive the way and his power to work out the deliverance <hi type="italic">out of temptation,</hi> to prevent their falling into sin and their being ruined by their troubles. And surely, if he can deliver out of temptation, he could keep from falling into it if he did not see such trials to be necessary. (4.) God makes a very great difference in his dealings with the godly and the wicked. When he saves his people from destruction, he delivers over his enemies to deserved ruin. The unjust has no share in the salvation God works out for the righteous. The wicked are <hi type="italic">reserved to the day of judgment.</hi> Here we see, [1.] There is a day of judgment. <hi type="italic">God has appointed a day wherein he will judge the world.</hi> [2.] The preservation of impenitent sinners is only a reserving of them to the day of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God.
entries.eb80ced0402c5f30d827d701b6c8aa1612bd9826: <div eID="gen33579" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">False Teachers. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 67.)</title> <div sID="gen33580" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> But chiefly them that walk after the flesh in the lust of uncleanness, and despise government. Presumptuous <hi type="italic">are they,</hi> selfwilled, they are not afraid to speak evil of dignities. <hi type="super">11</hi> Whereas angels, which are greater in power and might, bring not railing accusation against them before the Lord. 12 But these, as natural brute beasts, made to be taken and destroyed, speak evil of the things that they understand not; and shall utterly perish in their own corruption; <hi type="super">13</hi> And shall receive the reward of unrighteousness, <hi type="italic">as</hi> they that count it pleasure to riot in the day time. Spots <hi type="italic">they are</hi> and blemishes, sporting themselves with their own deceivings while they feast with you; <hi type="super">14</hi> Having eyes full of adultery, and that cannot cease from sin; beguiling unstable souls: a heart they have exercised with covetous practices; cursed children: <hi type="super">15</hi> Which have forsaken the right way, and are gone astray, following the way of Balaam <hi type="italic">the son</hi> of Bosor, who loved the wages of unrighteousness; <hi type="super">16</hi> But was rebuked for his iniquity: the dumb ass speaking with man's voice forbad the madness of the prophet. <hi type="super">17</hi> These are wells without water, clouds that are carried with a tempest; to whom the mist of darkness is reserved for ever. <hi type="super">18</hi> For when they speak great swelling <hi type="italic">words</hi> of vanity, they allure through the lusts of the flesh, <hi type="italic">through much</hi> wantonness, those that were clean escaped from them who live in error. <hi type="super">19</hi> While they promise them liberty, they themselves are the servants of corruption: for of whom a man is overcome, of the same is he brought in bondage. <hi type="super">20</hi> For if after they have escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, they are again entangled therein, and overcome, the latter end is worse with them than the beginning. <hi type="super">21</hi> For it had been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness, than, after they have known <hi type="italic">it,</hi> to turn from the holy commandment delivered unto them. 22 But it is happened unto them according to the true proverb, The dog <hi type="italic">is</hi> turned to his own vomit again; and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire. <div eID="gen33580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33581" type="x-p"/> The apostle's design being to warn us of, and arm us against, seducers, he now returns to discourse more particularly of them, and give us an account of their character and conduct, which abundantly justifies the righteous Judge of the world in reserving them in an especial manner for the most severe and heavy doom, as Cain is taken under special protection that he might be kept for uncommon vengeance. But why will God thus deal with these false teachers? This he shows in what follows. <div eID="gen33581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33582" type="x-p"/> I. <hi type="italic">These walk after the flesh;</hi> they follow the devices and desires of their own hearts, they give up themselves to the conduct of their own fleshly mind, refusing to make their reason stoop to divine revelation, and to <hi type="italic">bring every thought to the obedience of Christ;</hi> they, in their lives, act directly contrary to God's righteous precepts, and comply with the demands of corrupt nature. Evil opinions are often accompanied with evil practices; and those who are for propagating error are for improving in wickedness. They will not sit down contented in the measure of iniquity to which they have attained, nor is it enough for them to stand up, and maintain, and defend, what wickedness they have already committed, but they <hi type="italic">walk after the flesh,</hi> they go on in their sinful course, and increase unto more ungodliness and greater degrees of impurity and uncleanness too; they also pour contempt on those whom God has set in authority over them and requires them to honour. These therefore despise <hi type="italic">the ordinance of God,</hi> and we need not wonder at it, for they are bold and daring, obstinate and refractory, and will not only cherish contempt in their hearts, but with their tongues will utter slanderous and reproachful words of those who are set over them. <div eID="gen33582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33583" type="x-p"/> II. This he aggravates, by setting forth the very different conduct of more excellent creatures, even the <hi type="italic">angels,</hi> of whom observe, 1. They <hi type="italic">are greater in power and might,</hi> and that even than those who are clothed with authority and power among the sons of men, and much more than those false teachers who are slanderous revilers of magistrates and governors; the good angels vastly exceed us in all natural and moral excellences, in strength, understanding, and holiness too. 2. Good angels are accusers of sinful creatures, either of their own kind, or ours, or both. Those who are allowed to behold the face of God, and stand before his throne, cannot but have a zeal for his honour, and accuse and blame those who dishonour him. 3. <hi type="italic">Angels bring</hi> their <hi type="italic">accusations</hi> of sinful creatures <hi type="italic">before the Lord;</hi> they do not publish their faults, and tell their crimes to their fellow-creatures, in a way of calumny and slander; but it is before the Lord, who is the Judge, and will be the avenger, of all impiety and injustice. 4. Good angels mingle no bitter revilings nor base reproaches with any of the accusations or charges they bring against the wickedest and worst of criminals. Let us, who pray that God's <hi type="italic">will may be done on earth as it is in heaven,</hi> imitate the angels in this particular; if we complain of wicked men, let it be to God, and that not with rage and reviling, but with compassion and composedness of mind, that may evidence that we belong to him who is meek and merciful. <div eID="gen33583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33584" type="x-p"/> III. The apostle, having shown (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.11">v. 11</reference>) how unlike seducing teachers are to the most excellent creatures, proceeds (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.12">v. 12</reference>) to show how like they are to the most inferior: they are <hi type="italic">like the horse and mule, which have no understanding;</hi> they are <hi type="italic">as natural brute beasts, made to be taken and destroyed.</hi> Men, under the power of sin, are so far from observing divine revelation that they do not exercise reason, nor act according to the direction thereof. They <hi type="italic">walk by sight, and not by faith,</hi> and judge of things according to their senses; as these represent things pleasant and agreeable, so they must be approved and esteemed. Brute-creatures follow the instinct of their sensitive appetite, and sinful man follows the inclination of his carnal mind; these refuse to employ the understanding and reason God has given them, and so are ignorant of what they might and ought to know; and therefore observe, 1. Ignorance is the cause of evil-speaking; and, 2. Destruction will be the effect of it. These persons shall be utterly destroyed in their own corruption. Their vices not only expose them to the wrath of God in another world, but often bring them to misery and ruin in this life; and surely such impudent offenders, who <hi type="italic">glory in their shame,</hi> and to whom openness in sin is an improvement of the pleasure of sinning, most justly deserve all the plagues of this life and the pains of the next in the greatest extremity. Therefore whatever they meet with is the just <hi type="italic">reward of their unrighteousness.</hi> Such sinners as sport themselves in mischief deceive themselves and disgrace all they belong to, for by one sort of sins they prepare themselves for another; their extravagant feastings, their intemperance in eating and drinking, bring them to commit all manner of lewdness, so that their <hi type="italic">eyes are full of adultery,</hi> their wanton looks show their own impure lusts and are designed and directed to kindle the like in others; and this is what they <hi type="italic">cannot cease</hi> from—the heart is insatiate in lusting and the eye incessant in looking after what may gratify their unclean desires, and those who are themselves impudent and incessant in sin are very diligent and often successful in deceiving others and drawing others into the same excess of riot. But here observe who those are who are in the greatest danger of being led away into error and impiety, even the <hi type="italic">unstable.</hi> Those whose hearts are not established with grace are easily turned into the way of sin, or else such sensual wretches would not be able to prevail upon them, for these are not only riotous and lascivious, but <hi type="italic">covetous</hi> also, and these practices their hearts are exercised with; they pant after riches, and the desire of their souls is to the wealth of this world: it is a considerable part of their work to contrive to get wealth; in this their hearts are exercised, and then they execute their projects; and, if men abandon themselves to all sorts of lusts, we cannot wonder that the apostle should call them <hi type="italic">cursed children,</hi> for they are liable to the curse of God denounced against such <hi type="italic">ungodly and unrighteous men,</hi> and they bring a curse upon all who hearken and adhere to them. <div eID="gen33584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33585" type="x-p"/> IV. The apostle (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.15-2Pet.2.16">v. 15, 16</reference>) proves that they are <hi type="italic">cursed children,</hi> even such covetous persons as <hi type="italic">the Lord abhors,</hi> by showing, 1. They <hi type="italic">have forsaken the right way;</hi> and it cannot be but such self-seekers must be out of the right way, which is a self-denying way. 2. They have gone into a wrong way: they have erred and strayed from the way of life, and gone over into the path which leads to death, and takes hold of hell; and this he makes out by showing it to be <hi type="italic">the way of Balaam, the son of Bosor.</hi> (1.) That is a way of unrighteousness into which men are led by the wages of unrighteousness. (2.) Outward temporal good things are the wages sinners expect and promise themselves, though they are often disappointed. (3.) The inordinate love of the good things of this world turns men out of the way which leads to the unspeakably better things of another life; the love of riches and honour turned Balaam out of the way of his duty, although he knew that the way he took displeased the Lord. (4.) Those who from the same principle are guilty of the same practices with notorious sinners are, in the judgment of God, the followers of such vile offenders, and therefore must reckon upon being at last where they are: <hi type="italic">they shall have their portion</hi> with those in another world whom they imitated in this. (5.) Heinous and hardened sinners sometimes meet with rebukes for their iniquity. God stops them in their way, and opens the mouth of conscience, or by some startling providence startles and affrights them. (6.) Though some more uncommon and extraordinary rebuke may for a little while cool men's courage, and hinder their violent progress in the way of sin, it will not make them forsake the way of iniquity and go over into the way of holiness. If rebuking a sinner for his iniquity could have made a man return to his duty, surely the rebuke of Balaam must have produced this effect; for here is a surprising miracle wrought: <hi type="italic">the dumb ass,</hi> in whose mouth no man can expect to meet with reproof, is enabled to speak, and that with a human voice, and to her owner and master (who is here called a <hi type="italic">prophet,</hi> for the Lord appeared and spoke sometimes to him, <reference osisRef="Num.22.23-Num.22.24">Num. xxii. 23, 24</reference>, but indeed he was among the prophets of the Lord as Judas among the apostles of Jesus Christ), and she exposes <hi type="italic">the madness</hi> of his conduct and opposes his going on in this evil way, and yet all in vain. Those who will not yield to usual methods of reproof will be but little influenced by miraculous appearances to turn them from their sinful courses. Balaam was indeed restrained from actually <hi type="italic">cursing the people,</hi> but he had so strong a desire after the honours and riches that were promised him that he went as far as he could, and did his utmost to get from under the restraint that was upon him. <div eID="gen33585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33586" type="x-p"/> V. The apostle proceeds (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.17">v. 17</reference>) to a further description of seducing teachers, whom he sets forth, <div eID="gen33586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33587" type="x-p"/> 1. As <hi type="italic">wells,</hi> or fountains, <hi type="italic">without water.</hi> Observe, (1.) Ministers should be as wells or fountains, where the people may find instruction, direction, and comfort; but (2.) False teachers have nothing of this to impart to those who consult them: the word of truth is the water of life, which refreshes the souls that receive it; but these deceivers are set upon spreading and promoting error, and therefore are set forth as empty, because there is no truth in them. In vain then are all our expectations of being fed and filled with knowledge and understanding by those who are themselves ignorant and empty. <div eID="gen33587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33588" type="x-p"/> 2. As <hi type="italic">clouds carried with a tempest.</hi> When we see a cloud we expect a refreshing shower from it; but these are clouds which yield no rain, for they are driven with the wind, but not of the Spirit, but the stormy wind or tempest of their own ambition and covetousness. They espouse and spread those opinions that will procure most applause and advantage to themselves; and as clouds obstruct the light of the sun, and darken the air, so do these <hi type="italic">darken counsel by words without knowledge</hi> and wherein there is no truth; and, seeing these men are for promoting darkness in this world, it is very just that the mist of darkness should be their portion in the next. Utter darkness was prepared for the devil, the great deceiver, and his angels, those instruments that he uses to turn men from the truth, and therefore for them it is reserved, and that for ever; the fire of hell is everlasting, and the smoke of the bottomless pit rises up for ever and ever. And it is just with God to deal thus with them, because (1.) They allure those they deal with, and draw them into a net, or catch them as men do fish; and, (2.) It is <hi type="italic">with great swelling words of vanity,</hi> lofty expressions, which have a great sound, but little sense. (3.) They work upon <hi type="italic">the corrupt affections</hi> and <hi type="italic">carnal fleshly lusts of men,</hi> proposing what is grateful to them. And, (4.) They seduce persons who in reality avoided and kept at a distance from those who spread and those who embraced hurtful and destructive errors. Observe, [1.] By application and industry men attain a skilfulness and dexterity in promoting error. They are as artful and as successful as the fisher, who makes angling his daily employment. The business of these men is to draw disciples after them, and in their methods and management there are some things worth observing, how they suit their bait to those they desire to catch. [2.] Erroneous teachers have a peculiar advantage to win men over to them, because they have sensual pleasure to take them with; where as the ministers of Christ put men upon self-denial, and the mortifying of those lusts that others gratify and please: wonder not therefore that truth prevails no more, or that errors spread so much. [3.] Persons who have for a while adhered to the truth, and kept clear of errors, may by the subtlety and industry of seducers be so far deceived as to fall into those errors they had for a while <hi type="italic">clean escaped.</hi> "Be therefore always upon your guard, maintain a godly jealousy of yourselves, search the scriptures, pray for the Spirit to instruct and establish you in the truth, walk humbly with God, and watch against every thing that may provoke him to give you up to a reprobate mind, that you may not be taken with the fair and specious pretences of these false teachers, who promise liberty to all who will hearken to them, not true Christian liberty for the service of God, but a licentiousness in sin, to follow the devices and desires of their own hearts." To prevent these men's gaining proselytes, he tells us that, in the midst of all their talk of liberty, they themselves are the vilest slaves, for they are the servants of corruption; their own lusts have gotten a complete victory over them, and they are actually in bondage to them, making <hi type="italic">provision for the flesh,</hi> to satisfy its cravings, comply with its directions, and obey its commands. Their minds and hearts are so far corrupted and depraved that they have neither power nor will to refuse the task that is imposed on them. They are conquered and captivated by their spiritual enemies, and yield their members servants of unrighteousness: and what a shame it is to be overcome and commanded by those who are themselves <hi type="italic">the servants of corruption, and slaves to their own lusts!</hi> This consideration should prevent our being led away by these seducers; and to this he adds another (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.20">v. 20</reference>): it is not only a shame and disgrace to be seduced by those who are themselves the slaves of sin, and led captive by the devil at his pleasure, but it is a real detriment to those who have clean escaped from those who live in error, for hereby their latter end is made worse than their beginning. Here we see, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is an advantage to escape the pollutions of the world, to be kept from gross and scandalous sins, though men are not thoroughly converted and savingly changed; for hereby we are kept from grieving those who are truly serious and emboldening those who are openly profane; whereas, if we run with others to the same excess of riot and abandon ourselves to the sins of the age, we afflict and dishearten those who endeavour to walk as becomes the gospel, and strengthen the hands of those who are already engaged in open rebellion against the Most High, as well as alienate ourselves more from God, and harden our hearts against him. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Some men are, for a time, <hi type="italic">kept from the pollutions of the world, by the knowledge of Christ,</hi> who are not savingly renewed in the spirit of their mind. A religious education has restrained many whom the grace of God has not renewed: if we receive the light of the truth, and have a notional knowledge of Christ in our heads, it may be of some present service to us; but we must receive the love of the truth, and hide God's word in our heart, or it will not sanctify and save us. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Those who have, for a time, escaped the pollutions of the world, are at first ensnared and entangled by false teachers, who first perplex men with some plausible and specious objections against the truths of the gospel; and the more ignorant and unstable are hereby made to stagger, and brought to question the truth of doctrines they have received, because they cannot solve all the difficulties, nor answer all the objections, that are urged by these seducers. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> When men are once entangled, they are easily overcome; therefore should Christians keep close to the word of God, and watch against those who seek to perplex and bewilder them, and that because, if men who have once <hi type="italic">escaped are again entangled, the latter end is worse with them than the beginning.</hi> <div eID="gen33588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33589" type="x-p"/> VI. The apostle, in the <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.21-2Pet.2.22">last two verses of the chapter</reference>, sets himself to prove that a state of apostasy is worse than a state of ignorance; for it is a <hi type="italic">condemning of the way of righteousness,</hi> after they have had some knowledge of it, and expressed some liking to it; it carries in it a declaring that they have found some iniquity in the way of righteousness and some falsehood in the word of truth. Now to bring up such an evil report upon the good way of God, and such a false charge against the way of truth, must necessarily expose to the heaviest condemnation; the misery of such deserters of Christ and his gospel is more unavoidable and more intolerable than that of other offenders; for, 1. God is more highly provoked by those who by their conduct despise the gospel, as well as disobey the law, and who reproach and pour contempt upon God and his grace. 2. The devil more narrowly watches and more closely confines those whom he has recovered, after they had once gone off from him and professed to be the followers of the Lord Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.45">Matt. xii. 45</reference>); they are kept under a stronger guard, and no wonder it should be so when they have licked up their own vomit again, returning to the same errors and impieties that they had once cast off and seemed to detest and loathe, and wallowing in that filthiness from which they appeared once to be really cleansed. Well, if the scripture gives such an account of Christianity on the one hand, and of sin on the other, as we have here in <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.21-2Pet.2.22">these two verses</reference>, we certainly ought highly to approve of the former and persevere therein, because it is a way of righteousness, and a holy commandment, and to loathe and keep at the greatest distance from the latter because it is set forth as most offensive and abominable.  <chapter eID="2Pet.2"/> <div eID="gen33589" type="x-p"/>

entries.4e37009a687e1be7fdb648cd65702e89ac33234b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18853"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 2</title> <div sID="gen40346" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.1-2Pet.2.22">2Pe 2:1-22</reference>. False Teachers to Arise: Them Bad Practices and Sure Destruction, from Which the Godly Shall Be Delivered, as Lot Was.<div eID="gen40346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40347" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18853"/><hi type="bold">1. But--</hi>in contrast to the prophets "moved by the Holy Ghost" (<reference osisRef="2Pet.1.21">2Pe 1:21</reference>).<div eID="gen40347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40348" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">also--</hi>as well as the true prophets (<reference osisRef="2Pet.1.19-2Pet.1.21">2Pe 1:19-21</reference>). Paul had already testified the entrance of false prophets into the same churches.<div eID="gen40348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40349" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">among the people--</hi>Israel: he is writing to believing Israelites primarily (see on <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.1">1Pe 1:1</reference>). Such a "false prophet" was Balaam (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.15">2Pe 2:15</reference>).<div eID="gen40349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40350" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there shall be--</hi>Already symptoms of the evil were appearing (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.9-2Pet.2.22">2Pe 2:9-22</reference>; Jude 4-13).<div eID="gen40350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40351" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">false teachers--</hi>teachers of falsehood. In contrast to the true teachers, whom he exhorts his readers to give heed to (<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.2">2Pe 3:2</reference>).<div eID="gen40351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40352" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who--</hi>such as (literally, "the which") shall.<div eID="gen40352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40353" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">privily--</hi>not at first openly and directly, but by the way, bringing in error by the side of the true doctrine (so the Greek): Rome objects, Protestants cannot point out the exact date of the beginnings of the false doctrines superadded to the original truth; we answer, Peter foretells us it would be so, that the first introduction of them would be stealthy and unobserved (Jude 4).<div eID="gen40353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40354" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">damnable--</hi>literally, "of destruction"; entailing destruction (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.19">Php 3:19</reference>) on all who follow them.<div eID="gen40354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40355" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heresies--</hi>self-chosen doctrines, not emanating from God (compare "will-worship," <reference osisRef="Col.2.23">Col 2:23</reference>).<div eID="gen40355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40356" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">even--</hi>going even to such a length as to deny both in teaching and practice. Peter knew, by bitter repentance, what a fearful thing it is to deny the Lord (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.61">Lu 22:61</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.22.62">62</reference>).<div eID="gen40356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40357" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">denying--</hi>Him whom, above all others, they ought to confess.<div eID="gen40357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40358" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord--</hi>"Master and Owner" (Greek), compare Jude 4, Greek. Whom the true doctrine teaches to be their Owner by right of purchase. Literally, "denying Him who bought them (that He should be thereby), their Master."<div eID="gen40358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40359" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bought them--</hi>Even the ungodly were bought by His "precious blood." It shall be their bitterest self-reproach in hell, that, as far as Christ's redemption was concerned, they might have been saved. The denial of His propitiatory sacrifice is included in the meaning (compare <reference osisRef="1John.4.3">1Jo 4:3</reference>).<div eID="gen40359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40360" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bring upon themselves--</hi>compare "God bringing in the flood upon the world," <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.5">2Pe 2:5</reference>. Man brings upon himself the vengeance which God brings upon him.<div eID="gen40360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40361" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">swift--</hi>swiftly descending: as the Lord's coming shall be swift and sudden. As the ground swallowed up Korah and Dathan, and "they went down quick into the pit." Compare Jude 11, which is akin to this passage. <div eID="gen40361" type="x-p"/>
entries.e0c2388323b8599c95ec1a2cf3d6e9eb40ccd082: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18854"/><div sID="gen40362" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18854"/><hi type="bold">2. follow--</hi>out: so the Greek.<div eID="gen40362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40363" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pernicious ways--</hi>The oldest manuscripts and Vulgate read, "licentiousness" (Jude 4). False doctrine and immoral practice generally go together (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.18">2Pe 2:18</reference>, 19).<div eID="gen40363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40364" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by reason of whom--</hi>"on account of whom," namely, the followers of the false teachers.<div eID="gen40364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40365" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the way of truth shall be evil spoken of--</hi>"blasphemed" by those without, who shall lay on Christianity itself the blame of its professors' evil practice. Contrast <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.12">1Pe 2:12</reference>. <div eID="gen40365" type="x-p"/>
entries.8ccdde21726972efab13e7ef78b2c9afc7cf390a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18855"/><div sID="gen40366" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18855"/><hi type="bold">3. through, &c.--</hi>Greek, "IN covetousness" as their element (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.14">2Pe 2:14</reference>, end). Contrast <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.20">2Co 11:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.17">12:17</reference>.<div eID="gen40366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40367" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of a long time--</hi>in God's eternal purpose. "Before of old ordained to condemnation" (Jude 4).<div eID="gen40367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40368" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lingereth not--</hi>though sinners think it lingers; "is not idle."<div eID="gen40368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40369" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">damnation--</hi>Greek, "destruction" (see on <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.1">2Pe 2:1</reference>). Personified.<div eID="gen40369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40370" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">slumbereth not--</hi>though sinners slumber. <div eID="gen40370" type="x-p"/>
entries.ec81846f50054f7e3125c2992522ee5906a06939: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18856"/><div sID="gen40371" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18856"/><hi type="bold">4. if--</hi>The apodosis or consequent member of the sentence is not expressed, but is virtually contained in <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.9">2Pe 2:9</reference>. If God in past time has punished the ungodly and saved His people, He will be sure to do so also in our days (compare end of <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.3">2Pe 2:3</reference>).<div eID="gen40371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40372" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">angels--</hi>the highest of intelligent creatures (compare with this verse, Jude 6), yet not spared when they sinned.<div eID="gen40372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40373" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hell--</hi>Greek, "Tartarus": nowhere else in New Testament or the Septuagint: equivalent to the usual Greek, "Gehenna." Not inconsistent with <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.8">1Pe 5:8</reference>; for though their final doom is hell, yet for a time they are permitted to roam beyond it in "the darkness of this world." Slaves of Tartarus (called "the abyss," or "deep," <reference osisRef="Luke.8.31">Lu 8:31</reference>; "the bottomless pit," <reference osisRef="Rev.9.11">Re 9:11</reference>) may also come upon earth. Step by step they are given to Tartarus, until at last they shall be wholly bound to it.<div eID="gen40373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40374" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">delivered--</hi>as the judge delivers the condemned prisoner to the officers (<reference osisRef="Rev.20.2">Re 20:2</reference>).<div eID="gen40374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40375" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">into chains--</hi>(Jude 6). The oldest manuscripts read, "dens," as Alford translates: the Greek, however, may, in Hellenistic Greek, mean "chains," as Jude expresses it. They are "reserved" unto hell's "mist of darkness" as their final "judgment" or doom, and meanwhile their exclusion from the light of heaven is begun. So the ungodly were considered as virtually "in prison," though at large on the earth, from the moment that God's sentence went forth, though not executed till one hundred twenty years after. <div eID="gen40375" type="x-p"/>
entries.eb6a209b5ffa6c7ab984c9011d3828ca869017b0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18857"/><div sID="gen40376" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18857"/><hi type="bold">5. eighth--</hi>that is, Noah, and seven others. Contrasted with the densely peopled "world of the ungodly."<div eID="gen40376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40377" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">preacher--</hi>not only "righteous" himself (compare <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.8">2Pe 2:8</reference>), but also "a preacher of righteousness": adduced by Peter against the licentiousness of the false teachers (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.2">2Pe 2:2</reference>) who have no prospect before them but destruction, even as it overtook the ungodly world in Noah's days. <div eID="gen40377" type="x-p"/>
entries.688c8507c405315546b13605d20b7638c32bf132: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18858"/><div sID="gen40378" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18858"/><hi type="bold">6. with, &c.--</hi>"TO overthrow" [Alford].<div eID="gen40378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40379" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ensample--</hi>"of (the fate that should befall) those who in after-time should live ungodly." Compare Jude 7, "set forth for an example." <div eID="gen40379" type="x-p"/>
entries.30dc7a65b01578dac4449a01e46b76ccf4ef7f6e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18859"/><div sID="gen40380" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18859"/><hi type="bold">7. just--</hi>righteous.<div eID="gen40380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40381" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">filthy conversation--</hi>literally, "behavior in licentiousness" (<reference osisRef="Gen.19.5">Ge 19:5</reference>).<div eID="gen40381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40382" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the wicked--</hi>Greek, "lawless": who set at defiance the laws of nature, as well as man and God. The Lord reminds us of Lot's faithfulness, but not of his sin in the cave: so in Rahab's case. <div eID="gen40382" type="x-p"/>
entries.f1cce204c42aa4f6bd6d498a19d08bd210351c2e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18860"/><div sID="gen40383" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18860"/><hi type="bold">8. vexed--</hi>Greek, "tormented." <div eID="gen40383" type="x-p"/>
entries.ce96376279ed2358d959931ef35811e0c07a637b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18861"/><div sID="gen40384" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18861"/><hi type="bold">9. knoweth how--</hi>He is at no loss for means, even when men see no escape.<div eID="gen40384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40385" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">out of--</hi>not actually from.<div eID="gen40385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40386" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">temptations--</hi>trials.<div eID="gen40386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40387" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to be punished--</hi>Greek, "being punished": as the fallen angels (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.4">2Pe 2:4</reference>), actually under sentence, and awaiting its final execution. Sin is already its own penalty; hell will be its full development. <div eID="gen40387" type="x-p"/>
entries.fd28e758fb6a668f1617ad66d243dcda2c603762: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18862"/><div sID="gen40388" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18862"/><hi type="bold">10. chiefly--</hi>They especially will be punished (Jude 8).<div eID="gen40388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40389" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">after--</hi>following after.<div eID="gen40389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40390" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lust of uncleanness--</hi>defilement: "hankering after polluting and unlawful use of the flesh" [Alford].<div eID="gen40390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40391" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">government--</hi>Greek, "lordship," "dominion" (Jude 8).<div eID="gen40391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40392" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Presumptuous--</hi>Greek, "Darers." Self-will begets presumption. Presumptuously daring.<div eID="gen40392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40393" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">are not afraid--</hi>though they are so insignificant in might; Greek, "tremble not" (Jude 8, end).<div eID="gen40393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40394" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">speak evil of--</hi>Greek, "blaspheme."<div eID="gen40394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40395" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dignities--</hi>Greek, "glories." <div eID="gen40395" type="x-p"/>
entries.5a928816fd5a6214a46bbafbb517563d9c60177b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18863"/><div sID="gen40396" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18863"/><hi type="bold">11. which are--</hi>though they are.<div eID="gen40396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40397" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">greater--</hi>than these blasphemers. Jude instances Michael (Jude 9).<div eID="gen40397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40398" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">railing accusation--</hi>Greek, "blaspheming judgment" (Jude 9).<div eID="gen40398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40399" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">against them--</hi>against "dignities," as for instance, the fallen angels: once exalted, and still retaining traces of their former power and glory.<div eID="gen40399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40400" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before the Lord--</hi>In the presence of the Lord, the Judge, in reverence, they abstain from judgment [Bengel]. Judgment belongs to God, not the angels. How great is the dignity of the saints who, as Christ's assessors, shall hereafter judge angels! Meanwhile, railing judgments, though spoken with truth, against dignities, as being uttered irreverently, are of the nature of "blasphemies" (Greek, <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.4">1Co 4:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.5">5</reference>). If superior angels dare not, as being in the presence of God, the Judge, speak evil even of the bad angels, how awful the presumption of those who speak evil blasphemously of good "dignities." <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.7">2Sa 16:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.8">8</reference>, Shimei; <reference osisRef="Num.16.2">Nu 16:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.16.3">3</reference>, Korah, &c., referred to also in Jude 11; <reference osisRef="Num.12.8">Nu 12:8</reference>, "Were ye (Aaron and Miriam) not afraid to speak evil of My servant Moses?" The angels who sinned still retain the indelible impress of majesty. Satan is still "a strong man": "prince of this world"; and under him are "principalities, powers, rulers of the darkness of this world." We are to avoid irreverence in regard to them, not on their account, but on account of God. A warning to those who use Satan's name irreverently and in blasphemy. "When the ungodly curseth Satan, he curseth his own soul." <div eID="gen40400" type="x-p"/>
entries.2488ab8c88097655268a38932295e0e9ebc2fc8e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18864"/><div sID="gen40401" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18864"/>12. (Jude 19).<div eID="gen40401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40402" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">But--</hi>In contrast to the "angels," <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.11">2Pe 2:11</reference>.<div eID="gen40402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40403" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brute--</hi>Greek, "irrational." In contrast to angels that "excel in strength."<div eID="gen40403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40404" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">beasts--</hi>Greek, "animals" (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.49.20">Psa 49:20</reference>).<div eID="gen40404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40405" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">natural--</hi>transposed in the oldest manuscripts, "born natural," that is, born naturally so: being in their very nature (that is, naturally) as such (irrational animals), born to be taken and destroyed (Greek, "unto capture and destruction," or corruption, see on <reference osisRef="Gal.6.8">Ga 6:8</reference>; compare end of this verse, "shall perish," literally, "shall be corrupted," in their own corruption. Jude 10, naturally ... corrupt themselves," and so destroy themselves; for one and the same Greek word expresses corruption, the seed, and destruction, the developed fruit).<div eID="gen40405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40406" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">speak evil of--</hi>Greek, "in the case of things which they understand not." Compare the same presumption, the parent of subsequent Gnostic error, producing an opposite, though kindred, error, the worshipping of good angels": <reference osisRef="Col.2.18">Col 2:18</reference>, "intruding into those things which he hath not seen." <div eID="gen40406" type="x-p"/>
entries.6e7ed9c34a1e8db7fa83f3ca78b7fd9fe02e4019: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18865"/><div sID="gen40407" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18865"/><hi type="bold">13. receive--</hi>"shall carry off as their due."<div eID="gen40407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40408" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reward of--</hi>that is, for their "unrighteousness" [Alford]. Perhaps it is implied, unrighteousness shall be its own reward or punishment. "Wages of unrighteousness" (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.15">2Pe 2:15</reference>) has a different sense, namely, the earthly gain to be gotten by "unrighteousness."<div eID="gen40408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40409" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the daytime--</hi>Translate as Greek, "counting the luxury which is in the daytime (not restricted to night, as ordinary revelling. Or as Vulgate and Calvin, "the luxury which is but for a day": so <reference osisRef="Heb.11.25">He 11:25</reference>, "the pleasures of sin for a season"; and <reference osisRef="Heb.12.16">He 12:16</reference>, Esau) to be pleasure," that is, to be their chief good and highest enjoyment.<div eID="gen40409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40410" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Spots--</hi>in themselves.<div eID="gen40410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40411" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blemishes--</hi>disgraces: bringing blame (so the Greek) on the Church and on Christianity itself.<div eID="gen40411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40412" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sporting themselves--</hi>Greek, "luxuriating."<div eID="gen40412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40413" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with--</hi>Greek, "in."<div eID="gen40413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40414" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">deceivings--</hi>or else passively, "deceits": luxuries gotten by deceit. Compare <reference osisRef="Matt.13.22">Mt 13:22</reference>, "Deceitfulness of riches"; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.22">Ep 4:22</reference>, "Deceitful lusts." While deceiving others, they are deceived themselves. Compare with English Version, <reference osisRef="Phil.3.19">Php 3:19</reference>, "Whose glory is in their shame." "Their own" stands in opposition to "you": "While partaking of the love-feast (compare Jude 12) with you," they are at the same time "luxuriating in their own deceivings," or "deceits" (to which latter clause answers Jude 12, end: Peter presents the positive side, "they luxuriate in their own deceivings"; Jude, the negative, "feeding themselves without fear"). But several of the oldest manuscripts, Vulgate, Syriac, and Sahidic Versions read (as Jude), "In their own love-feasts": "their own" will then imply that they pervert the love-feasts so as to make them subserve their own self-indulgent purposes. <div eID="gen40414" type="x-p"/>
entries.0bedffa4ae4ed180a969c2e88c4dfe6b2fc50900: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18866"/><div sID="gen40415" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18866"/><hi type="bold">14. full of adultery--</hi>literally, "full of an adulteress," as though they carried about adulteresses always dwelling in their eyes: the eye being the avenue of lust [Horneius]. Bengel makes the adulteress who fills their eyes, to be "alluring desire."<div eID="gen40415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40416" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that cannot cease--</hi>"that cannot be made to cease from sin."<div eID="gen40416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40417" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">beguiling--</hi>"laying baits for."<div eID="gen40417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40418" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unstable--</hi>not firmly established in faith and piety.<div eID="gen40418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40419" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heart--</hi>not only the eyes, which are the channel, but the heart, the fountain head of lust. <reference osisRef="Job.31.7">Job 31:7</reference>, "Mine heart walked after mine eyes."<div eID="gen40419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40420" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">covetous practices--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read singular, "covetousness."<div eID="gen40420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40421" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cursed children--</hi>rather as Greek, "children of curse," that is, devoted to the curse. Cursing and covetousness, as in Balaam's case, often go together: the curse he designed for Israel fell on Israel's foes and on himself. True believers bless, and curse not, and so are blessed. <div eID="gen40421" type="x-p"/>
entries.5f8ac63fa0fbfa3146adcd5c1615fd8e7cafd0e6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18867"/><div sID="gen40422" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18867"/><hi type="bold">15. have--</hi>Some of the seducers are spoken of as already come, others as yet to come.<div eID="gen40422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40423" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">following--</hi>out: so the Greek.<div eID="gen40423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40424" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the way--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Num.22.23">Nu 22:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.22.32">32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.56.11">Is 56:11</reference>).<div eID="gen40424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40425" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">son of Bosor--</hi>the same as Beor (<reference osisRef="Num.22.5">Nu 22:5</reference>). This word was adopted, perhaps, because the kindred word Basar means flesh; and Balaam is justly termed son of carnality, as covetous, and the enticer of Israel to lust.<div eID="gen40425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40426" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">loved the wages of unrighteousness--</hi>and therefore wished (in order to gain them from Balak) to curse Israel whom God had blessed, and at last gave the hellish counsel that the only way to bring God's curse on Israel was to entice them to fleshly lust and idolatry, which often go together. <div eID="gen40426" type="x-p"/>
entries.b3c09620d859ee2252d2203f4767f7710d26808a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18868"/><div sID="gen40427" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18868"/><hi type="bold">16. was rebuked--</hi>Greek, "had a rebuke," or conviction; an exposure of his specious wickedness on his being tested (the root verb of the Greek noun means to "convict on testing").<div eID="gen40427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40428" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his--</hi>Greek, "his own": his own beast convicted him of his own iniquity.<div eID="gen40428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40429" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ass--</hi>literally, "beast of burden"; the ass was the ordinary animal used in riding in Palestine.<div eID="gen40429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40430" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dumb--</hi>Greek, "voiceless-speaking in man's voice"; marking the marvellous nature of the miracle.<div eID="gen40430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40431" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">forbade--</hi>literally, "hindered." It was not the words of the ass (for it merely deprecated his beating it), but the miraculous fact of its speaking at all, which withstood Balaam's perversity in desiring to go after God had forbidden him in the first instance. Thus indirectly the ass, and directly the angel, rebuked his worse than asinine obstinacy; the ass turned aside at the sight of the angel, but Balaam, after God had plainly said, Thou shalt not go, persevered in wishing to go for gain; thus the ass, in act, forbade his madness. How awful a contrast--a dumb beast forbidding an inspired prophet! <div eID="gen40431" type="x-p"/>
entries.c3b8cfd1875a0ae53844454caad81a8bcf0ec4b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18869"/><div sID="gen40432" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18869"/>17. (Jude 12, 13.)<div eID="gen40432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40433" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wells--</hi>"clouds" in Jude; both promising (compare <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.19">2Pe 2:19</reference>) water, but yielding none; so their "great swelling words" are found on trial to be but "vanity" (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.18">2Pe 2:18</reference>).<div eID="gen40433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40434" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">clouds--</hi>The oldest manuscripts and versions read, "mists," dark, and not transparent and bright as "clouds" often are, whence the latter term is applied sometimes to the saints; fit emblem of the children of darkness. "Clouds" is a transcriber's correction from Jude 12, where it is appropriate, "clouds ... without water" (promising what they do not perform); but not here, "mists driven along by a tempest."<div eID="gen40434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40435" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mist--</hi>blackness; "the chilling horror accompanying darkness" [Bengel]. <div eID="gen40435" type="x-p"/>
entries.2e9069cf42278e57da4c8e4812d7005caaf64f0a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18870"/><div sID="gen40436" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18870"/><hi type="bold">18. allure--</hi>Greek, "lay baits for."<div eID="gen40436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40437" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through--</hi>Greek, "in"; the lusts of the flesh being the element IN which they lay their baits.<div eID="gen40437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40438" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">much wantonness--</hi>Greek, "by licentiousness"; the bait which they lay.<div eID="gen40438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40439" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">clean escaped--</hi>Greek, "really escaped." But the oldest manuscripts and Vulgate read, "scarcely," or "for but a little time"; scarcely have they escaped from them who live in error (the ungodly world), when they are allured by these seducers into sin again (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.20">2Pe 2:20</reference>). <div eID="gen40439" type="x-p"/>
entries.efb3479e0858ca0e2de70f7e56d5739b8979c8c9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18871"/><div sID="gen40440" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18871"/><hi type="bold">19. promise ... liberty--</hi>(Christian)--These promises are instances of their "great swelling words" (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.18">2Pe 2:18</reference>). The liberty which they propose is such as fears not Satan, nor loathes the flesh. Pauline language, adopted by Peter here, and <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.16">1Pe 2:16</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.16">1Pe 2:16</reference>; (compare <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.15">2Pe 3:15</reference>; Ro 6:16-22; 8:<reference osisRef="Rom.15.21">15, 21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.5.1">Ga 5:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.5.13">13</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="John.8.34">Joh 8:34</reference>).<div eID="gen40440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40441" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">corruption--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.12">2Pe 2:12</reference>); "destroyed ... perish ... corruption."<div eID="gen40441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40442" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of whom--</hi>"by whatever ... by the same," &c. <div eID="gen40442" type="x-p"/>
entries.96c1b45612501560b5a9bb040b75ebf75640d0ad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18872"/><div sID="gen40443" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18872"/><hi type="bold">20. after they--</hi>the seducers "themselves" have escaped (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.19">2Pe 2:19</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="Heb.6.4-Heb.6.6">He 6:4-6</reference>).<div eID="gen40443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40444" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pollutions--</hi>which bring "corruption" (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.19">2Pe 2:19</reference>).<div eID="gen40444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40445" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through--</hi>Greek, "in."<div eID="gen40445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40446" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">knowledge--</hi>Greek, "full and accurate knowledge."<div eID="gen40446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40447" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ--</hi>solemnly expressing in full the great and gracious One from whom they fall.<div eID="gen40447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40448" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">latter end is worse ... than the beginning--</hi>Peter remembers Christ's words. "Worse" stands opposed to "better" (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.21">2Pe 2:21</reference>). <div eID="gen40448" type="x-p"/>
entries.e4847b0b9db075af295a61c49bb76fa9c9f58d23: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18873"/><div sID="gen40449" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18873"/><hi type="bold">21. the way of righteousness--</hi>"the way of truth" (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.2">2Pe 2:2</reference>). Christian doctrine, and "the knowledge of the Lord and Saviour."<div eID="gen40449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40450" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">turn--</hi>back again; so the Greek.<div eID="gen40450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40451" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from the holy commandment--</hi>the Gospel which enjoins holiness; in opposition to their corruption. "Holy," not that it makes holy, but because it ought to be kept inviolate [Tittmann].<div eID="gen40451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40452" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">delivered--</hi>once for all; admitting no turning back. <div eID="gen40452" type="x-p"/>
entries.f8bd01f71788a2a49cbbcd302edcd10f05112c0b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18874"/><div sID="gen40453" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18874"/><hi type="bold">22. But--</hi>You need not wonder at the event; for dogs and swine they were before, and dogs and swine they will continue. They "scarcely" (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.18">2Pe 2:18</reference>) have escaped from their filthy folly, when they again are entangled in it. Then they seduce others who have in like manner "for a little time escaped from them that live in error" (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.18">2Pe 2:18</reference>). Peter often quoted Proverbs in his First Epistle (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.7">1Pe 1:7</reference>; 2:17; 4:8, 18); another proof that both Epistles come from the same writer. <chapter eID="2Pet.2"/>

entries.1afaa3904afddb4d9bbcd7a66c4485e8dbe206f1: <div eID="gen54852" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen54853" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen54854" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen54854" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen54853" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen54855" type="x-p"/> False teachers foretold, who shall bring in destructive doctrines and shall pervert many, but at last be destroyed by the judgments of God, <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.1-2Pet.2.3">2Pet 2:1-3</reference>. Instances of God's judgments in the rebellious angels, <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.4">2Pet 2:4</reference>. In the antediluvians, <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.5">2Pet 2:5</reference>. In the cities of Sodom and Gomorrha, <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.6-2Pet.2.8">2Pet 2:6-8</reference>. The Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly, as well as to punish the ungodly, <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.9">2Pet 2:9</reference>. The character of those seducing teachers and their disciples; they are unclean, presumptuous, speak evil of dignities, adulterous, covetous, and cursed, <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.10-2Pet.2.14">2Pet 2:10-14</reference>. Have forsaken the right way, copy the conduct of Balaam, speak great swelling words, and pervert those who had escaped from error, <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.15-2Pet.2.19">2Pet 2:15-19</reference>. The miserable state of those who, having escaped the corruption that is in the world, have turned back like the dog to his vomit, and the washed swine to her wallowing in the mire, <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.20-2Pet.2.22">2Pet 2:20-22</reference>. <div eID="gen54855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54856" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen54856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54857" type="x-p"/> But there were false prophets - There were not only holy men of God among the Jews, who prophesied by Divine inspiration, but there were also false prophets, whose prophecies were from their own imagination, and perverted many. <div eID="gen54857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54858" type="x-p"/> As there shall be false teachers among you - At a very early period of the Christian Church many heresies sprung up; but the chief were those of the Ebionites, Cerinthians, Nicolaitans, Menandrians, and Gnostics, of whom many strange things have been spoken by the primitive fathers, and of whose opinions it is difficult to form any satisfactory view. They were, no doubt, bad enough, and their opponents in general have doubtless made them worse. By what name those were called of whom the apostle here speaks, we cannot tell. They were probably some sort of apostate Jews, or those called the Nicolaitans. See the preface. <div eID="gen54858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54859" type="x-p"/> Damnable heresies - Αἱρεσεις απωλειας· Heresies of destruction; such as, if followed, would lead a man to perdition. And these παρεισαξουσιν, they will bring in privately - cunningly, without making much noise, and as covertly as possible. It would be better to translate destructive heresies than damnable. <div eID="gen54859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54860" type="x-p"/> Denying the Lord that bought them - It is not certain whether God the Father be intended here, or our Lord Jesus Christ; for God is said to have purchased the Israelites, <reference osisRef="Exo.15.16">Exo 15:16</reference>, and to be the Father that had bought them, <reference osisRef="Deu.32.6">Deu 32:6</reference>, and the words may refer to these or such like passages; or they may point out Jesus Christ, who had bought them with his blood; and the heresies, or dangerous opinions, may mean such as opposed the Divinity of our Lord, or his meritorious and sacrificial death, or such opinions as bring upon those who hold them swift destruction. It seems, however, more natural to understand the Lord that bought them as applying to Christ, than otherwise; and if so, this is another proof, among many, <div eID="gen54860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54861" type="x-p"/> 1. That none can be saved but by Jesus Christ. <div eID="gen54861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54862" type="x-p"/> 2. That through their own wickedness some may perish for whom Christ died.
entries.87f9235139c86d609b1445287a19e75cae15544b: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen54862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54863" type="x-p"/> Many shall follow - Will follow, because determined to gratify their sinful propensities. <div eID="gen54863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54864" type="x-p"/> Pernicious ways - Ταις απωλειαις· Their destructions; i.e. the heresies of destruction, or destructive opinions, mentioned above. But instead of απωλειαις, destructions, ασελγειαις, lasciviousnesses or uncleannesses, is the reading of ABC, and upwards of sixty others, most of which are among the most ancient, correct, and authentic. This is the reading also of both the Syriac, all the Arabic, the Coptic, Ethiopic, Armenian, Slavonic, Vulgate, Chrysostom, Theophylact, Ecumenius, and Jerome. A very few, and those of little repute, have the word in the text. <div eID="gen54864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54865" type="x-p"/> The word lasciviousnesses is undoubtedly the true reading, and this points out what the nature of the heresies was: it was a sort of Antinomianism; they pampered and indulged the lusts of the flesh; and, if the Nicolaitans are meant, it is very applicable to them, for they taught the community of wives, etc. Griesbach has received this reading into the text. <div eID="gen54865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54866" type="x-p"/> By reason of whom - These were persons who professed Christianity; and because they were called Christians, and followed such abominable practices, the way of truth - the Christian religion, βλασφημηθησεται, was blasphemed. Had they called themselves by any name but that of Christ, his religion would not have suffered.
entries.ef34e219b5b56d6430e5ebf660b973033e59748f: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen54866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54867" type="x-p"/> And through covetousness - That they might get money to spend upon their lusts, with feigned words, πλαστοις λογοις, with counterfeit tales, false narrations, of pretended facts, lying miracles, fabulous legends. "In this single sentence," says Dr. Macknight, "there is a clear prediction of the iniquitous practices of those great merchants of souls, the Romish clergy, who have rated all crimes, even the most atrocious, at a fixed price; so that if their doctrine be true, whoever pays the price may commit the crime without hazarding his salvation." How the popish Church has made merchandise of souls, needs no particular explanation here. It was this abominable doctrine that showed to some, then in that Church, the absolute necessity of a reformation. <div eID="gen54867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54868" type="x-p"/> Whose judgment now of a long time - From the beginning God has condemned sin, and inflicted suitable punishments on transgressors; and has promised in his word, from the earliest ages, to pour out his indignation on the wicked. The punishment, therefore, so long ago predicted, shall fall on these impure and incorrigible sinners; and the condemnation which is denounced against them slumbers not - it is alert, it is on its way, it is hurrying on, and must soon overtake them.
entries.aa861b5680a842d049066ba7b633fd71f882def3: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen54868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54869" type="x-p"/> For if God spared not the angels - The angels were originally placed in a state of probation; some having fallen and some having stood proves this. How long that probation was to last to them, and what was the particular test of their fidelity, we know not; nor indeed do we know what was their sin; nor when nor how they fell. St. Jude says they kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation; which seems to indicate that they got discontented with their lot, and aspired to higher honors, or perhaps to celestial domination. The tradition of their fall is in all countries and in all religions, but the accounts given are various and contradictory; and no wonder, for we have no direct revelation on the subject. They kept not their first estate, and they sinned, is the sum of what we know on the subject; and here curiosity and conjecture are useless. <div eID="gen54869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54870" type="x-p"/> But cast them down to hell, and delivered them into chains of darkness - Αλλα σειραις ζοφου ταρταρωσας παρεδωκεν εις κρισιν τετηρημενους· But with chains of darkness confining them in Tartarus, delivered them over to be kept to judgment; or, sinking them into Tartarus, delivered them over into custody for punishment, to chains of darkness. Chains of darkness is a highly poetic expression. Darkness binds them on all hands; and so dense and strong is this darkness that it cannot be broken through; they cannot deliver themselves, nor be delivered by others. <div eID="gen54870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54871" type="x-p"/> As the word Tartarus is found nowhere else in the New Testament, nor does it appear in the Septuagint, we must have recourse to the Greek writers for its meaning. Mr. Parkhurst, under the word ταρταροω, has made some good collections from those writers, which I here subjoin. "The Scholiast on Aeschylus, Eumen., says: Pindar relates that Apollo overcame the Python by force; wherefore the earth endeavored ταρταρωσαι, to cast him into Tartarus. Tzetzes uses the same word, ταρταροω, for casting or sending into Tartarus; and the compound verb καταταρταρουν, is found in Apollodorus; in Didymus' Scholia on Homer; in Phurnutus, De Nat, Deor., p. 11, edit. Gale; and in the book Περι Ποταμων, which is extant among the works of Plutarch. And those whom Apollodorus styles καταταρταρωθεντας, he in the same breath calls ῥιφθεντας εις Ταρταρον, cast into Tartarus. Thus the learned Windet, in Pole's Synopsis. We may then, I think, safely assert that ταρταρωσας, in St. Peter, means not, as Mede (Works, fol., p. 23) interprets it, to adjudge to, but to cast into, Tartarus; ῥιπτειν εις Ταρταρον, as in Homer, cited below. And in order to know what was the precise intention of the apostle by this expression, we must inquire what is the accurate import of the term Ταρταρος. Now, it appears from a passage of Lucian, that by Ταρταρος was meant, in a physical sense, the bounds or verge of this material system; for, addressing himself to ΕΡΩΣ, Cupid or Love, he says: Συ γαρ εξ αφανους και κεχυμενης αμορφιας ΤΟ ΠΑΝ εμορφωσας, κ. τ. λ. 'Thou formedst the universe from its confused and chaotic state; and, after separating and dispersing the circumfused chaos, in which, as in one common sepulchre, the whole world lay buried, thou drovest it to the confines or recesses of outer Tartarus - 'Where iron gates and bars of solid brass <div eID="gen54871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54872" type="x-p"/> Keep it in durance irrefrangible, <div eID="gen54872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54873" type="x-p"/> And its return prohibit.' "The ancient Greeks appear to have received, by tradition, an account of the punishment of the 'fallen angels,' and of bad men after death; and their poets did, in conformity I presume with that account, make Tartarus the place where the giants who rebelled against Jupiter, and the souls of the wicked, were confined. 'Here,' saith Hesiod, Theogon., lin. 720, 1, 'the rebellious Titans were bound in penal chains.' Τοσσον ενερθ' ὑπο γης, ὁσον ουρανος εστ'απο γαιης. Ισον γαρ τ' απο γης ες ΤΑΡΤΑΡΟΝ ηεροεντα. 'As far beneath the earth as earth from heaven; <div eID="gen54873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54874" type="x-p"/> For such the distance thence to Tartarus.' <div eID="gen54874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54875" type="x-p"/> Which description will very well agree with the proper sense of Tartarus, if we take the earth for the center of the material system, and reckon from our zenith, or the extremity of the heavens that is over our heads. But as the Greeks imagined the earth to be of a boundless depth, so it must not be dissembled that their poets speak of Tartarus as a vast pit or gulf in the bowels of it. Thus Hesiod in the same poem, lin. 119, calls it - ΤΑΡΤΑΡΑ τ' ηεροεντα μυχῳ χθονος ευρυοδειης· 'Black Tartarus, within earth's spacious womb.' "And Homer, Iliad viii., lin. 13, etc., introduces Jupiter threatening any of the gods who should presume to assist either the Greeks or the Trojans, that he should either come back wounded to heaven, or be sent to Tartarus. Η μιν ἑλων ῥιψω ες ΤΑΡΤΑΡΟΝ ηεροεντα, Τηλε μαλ', ἡχι βαθιστον ὑπο χθονος εστι βερεθρον, Ενθα σιδηρειαι τε πυλαι, και χαλκεος ουδος, Τοσσον ενερθ' αιδεω, ὁσον ονρανος εστ' απο γαιης. 'Or far, O far, from steep Olympus thrown, <div eID="gen54875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54876" type="x-p"/> Low in the deep Tartarean gulf shall groan. <div eID="gen54876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54877" type="x-p"/> That gulf which iron gates and brazen ground <div eID="gen54877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54878" type="x-p"/> Within the earth inexorably bound; <div eID="gen54878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54879" type="x-p"/> As deep beneath th' infernal center hurl'd, <div eID="gen54879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54880" type="x-p"/> As from that center to the ethereal world.' <div eID="gen54880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54881" type="x-p"/> Pope. 'Where, according to Homer's description, Iliad viii., lin. 480, 1, - - - Ουτ' αυγης ὑπεριονος ηελιοιο Τερποντ', ουτ' ανεμοισι· βαθυς δε τε ΤΑΡΤΑΡΟΣ αμφις. 'No sun e'er gilds the gloomy horrors there, <div eID="gen54881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54882" type="x-p"/> No cheerful gales refresh the lazy air, <div eID="gen54882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54883" type="x-p"/> But murky Tartarus extends around.' <div eID="gen54883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54884" type="x-p"/> Pope. "Or, in the language of the old Latin poet, (cited by Cicero, Tuscul., lib. i. cap. 15), <div eID="gen54884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54885" type="x-p"/> Ubi rigida constat crassa caligo inferum. "On the whole, then, ταρταρουν, in St. Peter, is the same as ῥιπτειν ες Ταρταρον, to throw into Tartarus, in Homer, only rectifying the poet's mistake of Tartarus being in the bowels of the earth, and recurring to the original sense of that word above explained, which when applied to spirits must be interpreted spiritually; and thus ταρταρωσας will import that God cast the apostate angels out of his presence into that ζοφος του σκοτους, blackness of darkness, (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.17">2Pet 2:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jde.1.13">Jde 1:13</reference>), where they will be for ever banished from the light of his countenance, and from the beatifying influence of the ever blessed Three, as truly as a person plunged into the torpid boundary of this created system would be from the light of the sun and the benign operations of the material heavens." By chains of darkness we are to understand a place of darkness and wretchedness, from which it is impossible for them to escape.
